title: Connect Four
prompt: Design the classes for a Connect Four game. Two players take turns dropping discs into a 7-column × 6-row grid. A disc falls to the lowest empty cell in the chosen column. The first player to align four of their discs horizontally, vertically, or diagonally wins. The game ends in a draw if the grid fills with no winner.

stages.title: Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: Clarify the requirements. What's in scope and what isn't?
stages.howToAnswer: Capture the rules tightly. Decide whether to scope: AI opponent, multi-game match, network play. State assumptions out loud.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Tic Tac Toe):
bullets: Two players alternate placing X and O on a 3x3 grid
A player wins by completing a row, column, or diagonal
Game ends in a draw if the grid fills with no winner
Out of Scope: UI, AI opponent, networking

must: Two players, alternating turns
Drop disc into a column → falls to lowest empty row
Win condition: 4 in a row (horizontal/vertical/diagonal)
Draw when grid is full
Reject moves into a full column
avoid: Building an AI opponent unless asked

stages.sampleAnswer:
Scope:
- 2 human players, alternating turns. Player 1 = RED, Player 2 = YELLOW.
- 7 columns × 6 rows. Discs fall to the lowest empty row in the chosen column.
- Win = 4 same-colored discs in a row, column, or diagonal.
- Draw if grid full with no winner.
- Reject moves into a full column.

Out of scope: AI opponent, networking, persistent rankings.
hints: Capture the rules tightly: turn order, winning, drawing, and rejected moves.
Decide explicit out-of-scope items up front. AI? Networking? Persistence?
Configurable dimensions and win length come up naturally — call them out as a 'should'.

stages.title: Entities & Relationships
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core entities and how do they relate?
stages.howToAnswer: Pick the orchestrator. Decide what owns the board state. Avoid an anaemic God class.

must: Game (orchestrator)
Board (grid state)
Player
Disc / Cell with color enum
avoid: Putting all logic on Game and treating Board as a dumb 2D array

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Game: orchestrates turns, holds the Board and the two Players, reports state.
- Board: owns the 2D cell grid. Knows how to drop a disc and how to check whether a recently-placed disc is part of a winning line.
- Player: { name, color }.
- Color: enum RED | YELLOW.
- Cell: holds Optional<Color>.

Game depends on Board and Player. Board is the rule-keeper for placement and win-detection.
hints: Pick the orchestrator before defining classes. What entity drives the game loop?
Avoid the God-class trap — what state belongs on Board, what belongs on Game?
Player and Color are easy to forget. What's the relationship between them?

stages.title: Class Design
stages.questionPrompt: Define the classes — fields and methods. Keep rules with the entity that owns the state.
stages.howToAnswer: Sketch each class with explicit method signatures and what they return / throw. Decide return type for `dropDisc` (e.g., enum: WIN/DRAW/CONTINUE).

exampleHints.headline: Example (Tic Tac Toe):
bullets: class Board: + place(row, col, player); + checkWin(...)
enum GameState { IN_PROGRESS, X_WINS, O_WINS, DRAW }

must: Board.dropDisc(column, color) returns the placed cell's row or throws on full column
Board.checkWin(row, col) → bool
Game.playMove(column) advances turn and returns the resulting state
Color enum
should: Board configurable via constructor (rows, cols, winLength)
avoid: Returning bool from playMove — too lossy for a UI to render

stages.sampleAnswer:
```
enum Color { RED, YELLOW }
enum GameState { IN_PROGRESS, RED_WINS, YELLOW_WINS, DRAW }

class Board(rows=6, cols=7, winLength=4):
  cells: Color?[rows][cols]
  heights: int[cols]   // next empty row per column
  dropDisc(col, color) -> (row, col):
    if heights[col] == rows: throw ColumnFullError
    row = heights[col]++
    cells[row][col] = color
    return (row, col)
  checkWin(row, col) -> bool:
    color = cells[row][col]
    for each direction (horiz, vert, two diagonals):
      count consecutive `color` cells through (row, col)
      if count >= winLength: return true
    return false
  isFull() -> bool: sum(heights) == rows * cols

class Player:
  name: str
  color: Color

class Game:
  board: Board
  players: [Player, Player]
  turn: int = 0
  state: GameState = IN_PROGRESS
  playMove(col) -> GameState:
    if state != IN_PROGRESS: throw GameOverError
    p = players[turn % 2]
    (row, col) = board.dropDisc(col, p.color)
    if board.checkWin(row, col):
      state = p.color == RED ? RED_WINS : YELLOW_WINS
    elif board.isFull():
      state = DRAW
    else:
      turn += 1
    return state
```
hints: Methods that affect game state should return a richer-than-bool result — what's the right shape?
Lift dimensions and win length to constructor parameters. What invariants hold at construction?
Where does win-checking live? On Board, on a separate WinChecker, or on Game? Justify.

stages.title: Implementation
stages.questionPrompt: Pseudo-code the win check and trace through one game.
stages.howToAnswer: Win check is the meaty method — write it carefully. Then trace a sample sequence: alternate moves, eventual win.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Tic Tac Toe):
bullets: checkWin(row, col): walk all 4 directions from the just-placed cell
Use a (dr, dc) helper to count consecutive same-player cells

must: Win check considers all 4 directions
Win check counts consecutive cells through the just-placed cell (not naive O(rows*cols) full scan)
Bounds-checked array access
should: Single helper that walks a (dx, dy) direction and counts matching cells
Trace through one win condition end-to-end
avoid: Recomputing the entire board on every move

stages.sampleAnswer:
```
checkWin(row, col):
  color = cells[row][col]
  directions = [(0,1), (1,0), (1,1), (1,-1)]
  for (dr, dc) in directions:
    count = 1
    count += walk(row, col, dr, dc, color)
    count += walk(row, col, -dr, -dc, color)
    if count >= winLength: return true
  return false

walk(row, col, dr, dc, color):
  count = 0
  r, c = row + dr, col + dc
  while 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols and cells[r][c] == color:
    count += 1
    r += dr; c += dc
  return count
```

Trace: P1 drops col=3 → (row=0, col=3, RED). checkWin walks all four directions from (0,3). All counts == 1 < 4 → IN_PROGRESS, turn flips. P2 drops col=3 → (1,3, YELLOW). … Eventually RED has discs at (0,0), (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) — checkWin from (3,3) walks (-1,-1) direction, finds 3 RED, total 4 → RED_WINS.
hints: Pseudocode the meaty method first — dropDisc + win-check. The rest is plumbing.
Bounds-check column input at the API boundary. What kind of error per case?
Trace one full game end-to-end (place 4 in a row) to flush off-by-ones.

stages.title: Extensibility
stages.questionPrompt: How would you extend this for: an AI opponent, an N-in-a-row variant (e.g., Connect 5), or networked play?
stages.howToAnswer: Stay high-level. Point at the seams in the design that make the change clean.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Tic Tac Toe):
bullets: AI opponent: Player becomes an interface; HumanPlayer / AIPlayer impls
N-in-a-row: Board already takes winLength — pass 5 instead of 3

must: AI opponent: Player becomes an interface; HumanPlayer / AIPlayer implementations
N-in-a-row: winLength is already a Board constructor parameter — done
should: Networked play: introduce a MoveSource abstraction (local input vs websocket)
avoid: Rewriting Board to support N-in-a-row when it already takes winLength

stages.sampleAnswer:
AI opponent: lift Player to an interface with `chooseColumn(board) -> int`. HumanPlayer prompts the UI; AIPlayer runs minimax / MCTS. Game just calls `currentPlayer.chooseColumn(board)`.

N-in-a-row: nothing to change — Board's constructor already accepts winLength. Pass 5 instead of 4.

Networked play: introduce a MoveSource abstraction. Local games use a LocalMoveSource (keyboard input). Networked games use a WebsocketMoveSource that blocks until a move arrives from the peer. Game.playMove stays the same; only the source of the column number changes. Authoritative state lives on a server-side Game; clients receive state diffs.
hints: Where are the seams in your design? Point at them, don't redesign.
AI opponent: what's the smallest abstraction that lets HumanPlayer and AIPlayer share a path?
Networked play: what's the minimal contract that both local and remote moves satisfy?

deepDives.title: Efficient win detection
deepDives.questionPrompt: How do you check for a win without scanning the whole board after every move?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: After dropDisc(col, color), let (r, c) be the placed cell. For each of the 4 directions ((dr,dc) ∈ {(0,1),(1,0),(1,1),(1,-1)}), walk both ways from (r,c) counting contiguous same-color cells. If forward + backward + 1 ≥ 4 in any direction, win. This is O(1) work per move (bounded by winLength on each side) versus O(rows × cols) for a naive full-board scan. It also gives you the winning cells for free, useful for highlighting in the UI.

must: Only check lines through the new disc
Walk outward in 4 directions, counting contiguous
should: Note the bounded O(winLength) cost per move
Mention returning the winning line for the caller
avoid: Re-scanning the whole board every turn

hints: After a move, only certain lines could possibly be winning. Which ones, exactly?
Walk outward in each direction from the new cell. What stops the walk?
What's the cost per move under your scheme? Compare it to the naive 'scan the whole board' approach.

deepDives.title: Error handling
deepDives.questionPrompt: What can go wrong on dropDisc, and how does each case surface to the caller?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Three cases: (1) Column out of range → IllegalArgumentException — programmer error, fail loudly. (2) Column full → throw ColumnFullException, a checked condition the caller is expected to handle by re-prompting the user. (3) Game already finished → return the existing terminal MoveResult instead of throwing, so callers in a tight loop don't have to special-case it. dropDisc returns a MoveResult enum (CONTINUE | WIN(color) | DRAW) rather than a bool — the caller always knows what state to render next.

must: Cover at least 3 distinct error or terminal cases
Decide throw vs typed return per case
Method returns richer-than-bool result
should: Differentiate programmer errors from user errors
avoid: Returning bool and forcing callers to query separately for state

hints: Categorize the error cases: programmer error, user error, terminal state. Each gets a different surface.
Returning `bool` from a state-mutating method usually loses information. What's a richer return type?
What about calling dropDisc on a finished game? Throw, return, or no-op?

deepDives.title: Configurable rules
deepDives.questionPrompt: How would you support arbitrary M-in-a-row on an arbitrary R × C board without rewriting the design?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Constructor: Board(rows, cols, winLength). Invariants enforced once: 1 ≤ winLength ≤ max(rows, cols). All grid sizing comes from these fields — no constants in dropDisc, checkWin, or rendering. winLength flows into the directional walk in checkWin. Game.takeTurn doesn't change at all. To play 5-in-a-row on a 9×9 board: `new Board(9, 9, 5)`. The AI Player abstraction from the extensibility section also just keeps working — `chooseColumn(board)` still receives the same Board contract.

must: Lift dimensions and winLength to constructor params
Win-detection uses winLength, not a literal 4
avoid: Magic numbers scattered through the code

hints: Where do magic numbers (4, 7, 6) currently live? Promote them to named constructor params.
Win-detection should already not hardcode 4 — verify that as a self-check.
Validate inputs once at construction. What's the bound on win length given board size?
